hypothesis: For a production multi-agent workflow handling operational tickets, introducing SRE-style observability (SLIs/SLOs, dashboards, alerts) plus a controlled prompt/tool tuning loop will (a) reduce user-flagged error rate and regression frequency, and (b) maintain or improve throughput and latency within defined SLOs, compared with an equivalent deployment that logs only raw events and does ad-hoc, non-metric-driven tuning.

baseline.description: Multi-agent workflow in production with minimal observability and ad-hoc improvements.
characteristics: Multi-agent orchestrator manages a simple operations workflow (e.g., internal IT or CX ticket triage and resolution).
Logging limited to raw event logs (e.g., JSON lines with timestamps, agent name, action) stored in a database or object store, without derived SLIs or structured evaluation.
No explicit SLIs/SLOs or error budgets; success judged qualitatively or via occasional manual report pulls.
No real-time alerts; issues are discovered via user complaints or periodic spot-checks.
Changes to prompts, tools, or routing are made manually and reactively, without A/B testing or canaries.
One static prompt/workflow configuration deployed to all traffic (no varianting).
User feedback is captured only via informal channels (e.g., email/Slack complaints) and not systematically tied to specific agent runs.

implementation_sketch.orchestrator: Python service using a task queue (e.g., Redis, RabbitMQ, or in-memory for local runs) to route tickets to 2–3 agents (router, resolver, reviewer).
agents: router_agent: classifies incoming requests and assigns category/priority.
resolver_agent: proposes actions or responses using tools (e.g., knowledge base search) and LLM calls.
reviewer_agent: optional final check that approves/edits responses.
implementation_sketch.logging: Append-only log (e.g., Postgres table or JSONL file) for each run_id with agent_name, step_index, raw_payload, timestamp, and status.
implementation_sketch.deployment_mode: Single environment (`prod-like`) processing all incoming workloads with one fixed configuration.

treatment.description: Same multi-agent workflow with explicit SLIs/SLOs, dashboards, alerting, and a structured, experiment-driven improvement loop (canaries and A/B tests) for prompts/tools/routing.
additions_over_baseline: Defined SLIs for the workflow, computed from logs and feedback, e.g.:
- `sli_success_rate`: share of agent sessions that complete without user override or critical error.
- `sli_user_flag_rate`: share of sessions explicitly flagged as incorrect or low quality.
- `sli_handoff_rate`: share of sessions escalated to humans.
SLOs and error budgets derived from SLIs, e.g.:
Streaming of key metrics into a time-series store (e.g., Prometheus/Influx/Postgres rollups) and a dashboard (e.g., Grafana/Metabase).
Automated alerts (e.g., email/Slack/webhook) triggered when SLOs are threatened (e.g., breach of 25–50% of error budget within 24h, or latency p95 above threshold).
Structured feedback capture per run_id: user flags (thumbs up/down), correction text, and overrides stored in a feedback table.
- Canary releases: route a small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5–10%) to a new config variant; auto-rollback if SLIs degrade beyond guardrail thresholds.
- A/B tests: split traffic between baseline config and tuned config and measure relative performance using the same SLIs.
Systematic prompt and tool tuning driven by observed metrics and labeled errors; each new config is versioned and tied to experiment IDs.
Improvement backlog that ingests metric anomalies, frequent error patterns, and user feedback, prioritized by impact and effort.

implementation_sketch.orchestrator: Same as baseline, extended with an experiment router layer that assigns each incoming ticket to a configuration arm (control or variant) based on experiment definitions.
config_variants: tuned_v2: improved prompts (e.g., clearer instructions, added chain-of-thought in tools-only channels), refined routing rules, or additional verification tool calls.
implementation_sketch.metrics_pipeline: Background worker or scheduled job that aggregates raw logs into metrics tables per 5-min or 1-hour bucket, tagged by variant_id and environment.
implementation_sketch.alerting: Stateless service or cron job evaluating rolling windows of SLIs vs. SLOs and triggering notifications when thresholds are breached.
implementation_sketch.dashboards: Pre-built charts (e.g., success_rate, user_flag_rate, latency_p95, handoff_rate, volume) broken down by variant_id, environment, and ticket category.

workloads.name: synthetic_ticket_stream
workloads.description: Scripted generator of internal support or operations tickets to provide a reproducible, controllable workload for both baseline and treatment.
characteristics: Tickets represented as JSON objects with fields: ticket_id, created_at, channel, category, difficulty, language, and text.
Categories (e.g., 'password_reset', 'access_request', 'billing_question', 'bug_report'), each with templates and controlled difficulty levels.
Ground truth labels for required_action and correct_response exist so that offline accuracy can be computed in addition to online user feedback.
Arrival process: default Poisson or fixed-rate process (e.g., N tickets per minute) to simulate varying load levels.
Random seed control to generate identical sequences of tickets for repeated experiments.
workloads.generation_outline: Provide a Python script in the repo that accepts seed, rate, duration, and output_path, and emits a newline-delimited JSON file of tickets.

workloads.name: human_in_the_loop_feedback
workloads.description: Optional workload using real users or annotators reviewing agent outputs and flagging errors.
characteristics: Same ticket schema as synthetic stream but tickets can be sourced from a sandboxed real system (e.g., exported IT/CX tickets with anonymization).
Annotators review agent outputs and label correctness (correct, partially_correct, incorrect), provide corrections, and mark severity (low, medium, high).
Used to validate that SLI-based metrics correspond to actual user-perceived quality and to refine evaluation heuristics.
workloads.notes: This workload is more variable and not fully deterministic; it complements, but does not replace, the synthetic workload for strict reproducibility.

shared_controls: Use the same orchestrator codebase, agent graph, and underlying LLM model/version for baseline and treatment during any specific run (no implicit model upgrades).
Use the same synthetic_ticket_stream with a fixed random seed and identical ticket sequences for comparability in offline replay experiments.
Process equivalent workload volumes and category mixes in baseline and treatment arms over the same wall-clock period for online experiments.
Keep hardware and infrastructure constant across arms (same instance types, concurrency limits, and network conditions as far as possible).
Disable any auto-tuning or vendor-side experimentation that could confound results (e.g., turn off unspecified model switching in provider dashboards where possible).
experiment_routing_controls: Use a deterministic experiment assignment function (e.g., hash(ticket_id) mod 100) to ensure stable traffic splits and avoid per-user flapping across arms.
Ensure minimum sample sizes per arm (e.g., at least 1,000 tickets per variant in a given experiment) before drawing conclusions.
Freeze configuration for each variant for the duration of a given experiment; version changes create new variant_ids.
data_quality_controls: Validate all incoming tickets and agent outputs conform to schemas before processing (reject or quarantine malformed entries).
Backfill metrics from raw logs to validate that online metric computations match offline recomputations.
Guard against leakage of ground truth labels to agents (labels must not be part of agent-visible context during experiments).

metrics.name: success_rate
metrics.definition: Number of sessions that complete without user override, critical error, or escalation / total sessions. Computed per variant and time window.

metrics.name: user_flag_rate
metrics.definition: Number of sessions where a user explicitly flags output as incorrect or low quality / total sessions. Requires feedback UI or annotation.

metrics.name: handoff_rate
metrics.definition: Number of sessions escalated to a human (reviewer intervention or manual takeover) / total sessions.

metrics.name: latency_p50
metrics.definition: Median end-to-end time from ticket creation to agent-produced response.

metrics.name: latency_p95
metrics.definition: 95th percentile end-to-end time from ticket creation to agent-produced response.

metrics.name: throughput
metrics.definition: Number of completed sessions per minute processed by the system under a given load.

metrics.name: offline_accuracy
metrics.definition: For synthetic tickets with ground truth actions/responses, share of sessions where agent output matches ground truth (exact or relaxed criteria).

metrics.name: prompt_tool_change_frequency
metrics.definition: Number of prompt, tool, or routing configuration versions promoted to production per calendar week.

metrics.name: regression_incidents
metrics.definition: Count of distinct incidents where a config change caused a statistically significant degradation in any primary SLI (e.g., success_rate, user_flag_rate) beyond defined guardrails, leading to a rollback or hotfix.

metrics.name: alert_volume
metrics.definition: Number of SLO or guardrail alerts raised per week, used to measure noise vs. signal in monitoring configuration.

metrics.name: engineer_time_on_triage
metrics.definition: Estimated engineering/operations time spent manually investigating production issues with the agent system.

primary: Treatment success_rate is at least 3 percentage points higher than baseline (e.g., from 0.90 to >= 0.93) with 95% confidence over a comparable workload.
Treatment user_flag_rate is at least 30% lower relative to baseline (e.g., from 0.10 to <= 0.07) without violating latency_p95 SLO.
secondary: Treatment latency_p95 is not worse than baseline by more than 20% (e.g., if baseline is 25s, treatment <= 30s) OR any increase is justified by materially better success_rate/user_flag_rate.
Treatment regression_incidents per week are lower than or equal to baseline, even as prompt_tool_change_frequency increases or remains similar.
Alert_volume is in a manageable range (e.g., 1–10 actionable alerts/week) with low proportion of false positives, qualitatively assessed.
Engineer_time_on_triage does not increase and ideally decreases by at least 20% compared to baseline after ramp-up.

failure_modes.name: metrics_regress_without_detection
failure_modes.description: Agent performance degrades (e.g., rising user_flag_rate) but monitoring and alerts fail to detect the issue or do so too late.
causes: SLIs not correctly computed or thresholds too loose.
Alerting windows too coarse to capture fast regressions.
Metrics pipeline failures (e.g., missing data, mislabeling of variant_id).
mitigations: Run regular metric integrity checks (e.g., compare aggregate counts between logs and metrics tables).
Start with conservative (tighter) SLO thresholds and adjust based on observed noise.
Implement synthetic canary checks that send known tickets with expected outcomes at a fixed cadence.

failure_modes.name: noisy_or_misleading_SLIs
failure_modes.description: SLIs do not correlate well with actual user satisfaction or business outcomes, leading to optimization in the wrong direction.
causes: Proxy metrics (e.g., handoff_rate) used as quality stands-in without validation.
Low engagement with feedback tools; silent dissatisfaction not captured.
Synthetic workload that is not representative of real production tickets.
mitigations: Correlate SLIs with human_in_the_loop_feedback and, where possible, business KPIs (e.g., CSAT, resolution time).
Periodically sample sessions for manual review and compare qualitative judgment vs. SLI classification.
Iteratively refine SLIs and consider multiple complementary metrics rather than a single one.

failure_modes.name: experiment_contamination
failure_modes.description: Traffic or configuration mixing leads to biased comparisons between baseline and treatment variants.
causes: Users or tickets switching variants mid-session due to non-stable assignment.
Configuration changes applied mid-experiment without re-versioning.
Shared downstream systems that apply variant-specific rules inconsistently.
mitigations: Use stable assignment based on ticket_id or user_id hashing.
Freeze configuration for each variant_id during experiments; create new variant_ids for changes.
Log variant_id and config_version with every event; exclude sessions with mid-stream variant changes during analysis.

failure_modes.name: overfitting_to_synthetic_workloads
failure_modes.description: System is tuned to perform well on synthetic tickets but does not generalize to messy, real-world tickets.
causes: Synthetic dataset too clean, narrow, or patternable.
Prompts inadvertently specialized to synthetic phrasing.
Lack of diverse real feedback incorporated into training loop.
mitigations: Periodically run experiments on real, anonymized datasets with human_in_the_loop_feedback.
Increase variability and noise in synthetic generator (typos, mixed languages, ambiguous phrasing).
Validate patterns on at least two distinct workloads (e.g., IT tickets and CX tickets) before codifying them broadly.

failure_modes.name: alert_fatigue
failure_modes.description: Too many non-actionable alerts cause operators to ignore or mute notifications, undermining reliability.
causes: Overly sensitive thresholds or short evaluation windows.
Alerts triggered on raw metrics rather than SLO-focused aggregates.
Multiple near-duplicate alerts for the same underlying issue.
mitigations: Prioritize a small set of SLO-based alerts for paging; use dashboards for secondary metrics.
Implement alert deduplication and suppression windows.
Regularly review alert history and retire or tune noisy conditions.

failure_modes.name: unsafe_or_unvetted_prompt_tool_changes
failure_modes.description: New prompts or tools deployed via experimentation introduce previously unseen failure modes (e.g., policy violations or security issues).
causes: Insufficient guardrails or review before enabling variants.
Lack of policy-compliance checks in evaluation pipeline.
Overreliance on SLIs that do not explicitly capture safety violations.
mitigations: Require human review and approval for new variants before canary rollout.
Include safety-focused checks (e.g., policy classifier, PII detection) as pre-deployment tests and as part of SLIs.
Limit canary traffic share and scope (e.g., safer categories only) until safety metrics are validated.

infrastructure: Runtime environment capable of running Python 3.10+ services (e.g., local Docker, Kubernetes, or a simple VM).
Access to at least one LLM endpoint (cloud API or self-hosted) with sufficient rate limits to handle test workloads.
Message queue or simple async processing mechanism (e.g., Redis, RabbitMQ, or in-process async tasks) for orchestrating agents.
Database for logs, metrics, and feedback (e.g., Postgres or SQLite for minimal setups).
Dashboarding/visualization tool (e.g., Grafana, Metabase, Superset, or even a Jupyter notebook for initial experiments).
Job scheduler or cron-like mechanism for periodic metric aggregation and SLO evaluation.
software_dependencies: Python libraries for HTTP and queues (e.g., requests/httpx, redis/pika).
ORM or database client (e.g., SQLAlchemy, psycopg2, sqlite3).
Metrics and logging libraries (e.g., structlog/loguru, prometheus_client or custom metric aggregator).
Experiment configuration management (e.g., YAML/JSON-based configs parsed by the orchestrator).
Optional: Containerization (Docker) for repeatable local and CI runs.
datasets: Synthetic_ticket_generator script with seed and parameter controls, stored in the repository.
Optional real or anonymized ticket datasets for advanced validation, clearly separated from the synthetic workload and documented regarding privacy constraints.
configurations: Baseline config file defining the default prompts, tools, and routing logic.
Treatment/tuned config files defining variant prompts, tools, routing, and guardrail policies.
SLO definition file listing SLIs, SLO thresholds, evaluation windows, and alerting channels.
Experiment definition file specifying experiment_id, variants, traffic splits, and start/end dates.

run_instructions: 1. Clone the repository and set up environment
- `git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/turn-your-company-into-an-agentic-organization.git`
- `cd turn-your-company-into-an-agentic-organization/experiments/014_operate_monitor_improve_mas`
- Create and activate a Python virtual environment.
- Install dependencies: `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
- Configure LLM API keys and database connection strings via environment variables or a local `.env` file (never commit secrets).
2. Initialize databases and schemas
- Run the migration or schema script to create tables for: `runs`, `events`, `metrics`, `feedback`, `experiments`, and `config_versions`.
- Verify connectivity by running a short health-check script that writes and reads a test record.
3. Generate a synthetic workload
- Execute the workload generator with fixed seed and parameters, for example:
`python generate_synthetic_tickets.py --seed 42 --rate 5 --duration-minutes 60 --output tickets_seed42.jsonl`
- Inspect the first few lines of the output file to confirm ticket structure and category distribution.
4. Run the baseline experiment (no advanced monitoring or tuning framework enabled)
- Configure the orchestrator to use `config/baseline_v1.yml` (or equivalent) and disable experiment routing.
- Start the orchestrator service.
- Replay the synthetic tickets into the system:
`python replay_tickets.py --input tickets_seed42.jsonl --mode baseline --concurrency 5`
- Allow the system to complete processing all tickets; monitor logs to ensure there are no unhandled errors.
- After completion, run the baseline metrics aggregation script:
`python compute_metrics.py --mode baseline --variant-id control_v1 --window all`
- Export metrics to a JSON or CSV file, e.g., `metrics_baseline_control_v1.json`.
5. Enable treatment features (monitoring, SLOs, alerts, and experiment framework)
- Deploy or enable the metrics aggregation pipeline and verify that SLIs (success_rate, user_flag_rate, latency_p95, etc.) are computed per run and per variant.
- Configure SLOs and alert thresholds in `config/slo_definitions.yml`.
- Set up dashboards by importing pre-defined dashboards or pointing your dashboarding tool to the metrics tables.
- Configure alerting endpoints (e.g., Slack webhook URL, email distribution list) in `config/alerting.yml`.
6. Run a canary release of a tuned variant (treatment)
- Create or adapt a tuned configuration `config/tuned_v2.yml` (prompt, tool, or routing improvements).
- Register an experiment in `config/experiments.yml` with a small canary traffic share, for example:
- experiment_id: `exp_014_canary_v2`
- variants: `control_v1` (90%), `tuned_v2` (10%)
- Start the orchestrator with experiment routing enabled.
- Replay the same synthetic tickets or generate a new workload with the same seed and volume profile:
`python replay_tickets.py --input tickets_seed42.jsonl --mode experiment --concurrency 5`
- Monitor dashboards and logs during the run; confirm that metrics are reported separately for `control_v1` and `tuned_v2`.
- Allow the canary to complete sufficient volume (e.g., at least 1,000 tickets in `tuned_v2`) before diagnosing results.
7. Evaluate canary guardrails and escalate to A/B test
- Run metrics analysis:
`python compute_metrics.py --mode experiment --experiment-id exp_014_canary_v2 --window all`
- Compare SLIs for `control_v1` vs. `tuned_v2` against guardrail thresholds (e.g., user_flag_rate not worse by more than X%, latency_p95 not above SLO).
- If metrics are within guardrails and show improvement or parity, update `config/experiments.yml` for an A/B test with a larger traffic share (e.g., 50/50).
- Re-run the experiment and recompute metrics after hitting target sample size.
8. Collect and analyze user or annotator feedback (optional but recommended)
- For a subset of runs, route agent outputs to human reviewers via a simple web UI or annotation script.
- Store their correctness labels and comments in the `feedback` table linked by run_id and variant_id.
- Run the evaluation script to correlate SLIs with human-labeled correctness:
`python analyze_feedback_correlation.py --experiment-id exp_014_canary_v2`
- Adjust SLI definitions or thresholds if they are shown to be poorly correlated with actual quality.
9. Build and prioritize an improvement backlog
- Run the error cluster analysis script to identify frequent failure patterns and categories:
`python cluster_errors.py --experiment-id exp_014_canary_v2`
- Export a ranked list of candidate improvements by estimated impact and frequency.
- Use this output to populate or update an improvement backlog (e.g., in a CSV file or your issue tracker).
10. Document results and prepare for replication
- Save all configuration files (baseline, tuned, SLOs, experiments) with clear version tags.
- Export final metrics, including confidence intervals where computed, to JSON files.
- Record any environment specifics (model versions, hardware specs, rate limits) in a README within the experiment folder.
- Optionally commit sanitized configuration and non-secret outputs back to the repository for others to reproduce, subject to your internal policies.

evidence_schema.description: Schema for storing and analyzing evidence from the experiment in a structured, reproducible manner.

fields.run_id: string, unique identifier for a single end-to-end ticket handling session.
fields.ticket_id: string, identifier of the ticket from synthetic or real workload.
fields.experiment_id: string, e.g., 'exp_014_canary_v2'; null if no experiment.
fields.config_version: string, hash or semantic version of prompts/tools/routing used.
fields.start_time: datetime, when processing of this ticket began.
fields.end_time: datetime, when processing completed or was aborted.

fields.agent_name: string, name of the agent (router, resolver, reviewer, etc.).
fields.step_index: integer, sequence order within the run.
fields.payload_summary: string or JSON, high-level description without sensitive content.
fields.latency_ms: integer, time spent for this step (if applicable).
fields.variant_id: string, redundancy for faster querying; should match run.variant_id.

fields.correction_text: string, optional corrected answer or instructions.

fields.category: string, ticket category defined in generator.
fields.required_action: JSON, structured representation of expected agent actions.
fields.reference_response: string, reference text or template considered correct.
fields.evaluation_method: enum: ['exact_match', 'semantic_similarity', 'rule_based'], describing how offline_accuracy should be computed.

fields.variant_id: string, variant this metric refers to.
fields.metric_name: string, one of the metric names defined above (e.g., 'success_rate').
fields.value: float, numeric value of the metric.
fields.window_seconds: integer, aggregation window size (e.g., 300 for 5 minutes, 86400 for daily).
fields.sample_size: integer, number of runs underlying this metric point.

fields.slo_eval_id: string, unique id for each SLO check.
fields.timestamp: datetime, when the evaluation was performed.
fields.experiment_id: string, optional, focus experiment; null for global SLOs.
fields.variant_id: string, optional; null for aggregated SLOs across variants.
fields.value: float, observed SLI value in this window.
fields.breached: boolean, true if SLO is violated within this evaluation.
fields.error_budget_consumed: float, fraction of error budget used in this window (0.0–1.0).

fields.slo_eval_id: string, foreign key to slo_evaluation.slo_eval_id, if alert is SLO-based.
fields.metric_name: string, metric that triggered the alert (if not SLO-based).
fields.value: float, observed metric value at alert time.
fields.message: string, human-readable description of the alert.
fields.status: enum: ['open', 'acknowledged', 'resolved'], lifecycle state of the alert.
fields.resolution_notes: string, description of the root cause and actions taken.

fields.config_version: string, unique identifier (e.g., semantic version or hash).
fields.created_at: datetime, when the configuration was created.
fields.description: string, short summary of changes vs. previous version.
fields.prompts: JSON, key prompt snippets or references (no secrets).
fields.tools: JSON, list of available tools and their configuration (e.g., endpoints, timeouts).
fields.routing_rules: JSON, description of routing and orchestration logic.
fields.safety_policies: JSON, description of safety and guardrail rules applied.

fields.description: string, purpose and design of the experiment.
fields.end_time: datetime, actual or planned end; null if ongoing.
fields.variants: JSON, mapping of variant_id to traffic share, e.g., {'control_v1': 0.9, 'tuned_v2': 0.1}.
fields.primary_metrics: JSON, list of metrics monitored for decision-making.
fields.decision_notes: string, explanation of how the decision was reached, referencing metric evidence.
